patch.description_long: In early February 2025, the Treasury Department confirmed that a member of the government-efficiency team had read-only access to code associated with its federal payment system. Reuters reported that Treasury identified technology executive Tom Krause as leading the review and that the system handles more than $6 trillion in annual disbursements, including Social Security and Medicare payments. The review was presented by Treasury as an effort to improve payment integrity. The access prompted scrutiny because the payment infrastructure supports large federal programs and obligations to millions of recipients. Treasury said no payments had been suspended, rejected, delayed, or rerouted as a result of the review. The supplied reporting describes read-only access to payment-system code; it does not establish that DOGE had unrestricted authority to alter transactions, that the access lacked legal authorization, or that a breach or fraud occurred. The review prompted scrutiny of sensitive payment infrastructure even though Treasury said it had not interrupted or rerouted disbursements.

patch.description_long: On July 15, 2024, U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon dismissed the federal classified-documents indictment against Donald Trump and co-defendants Walt Nauta and Carlos De Oliveira. Cannon accepted their argument that Attorney General Merrick Garland lacked statutory authority to appoint special counsel Jack Smith and also found the special counsel’s funding unlawful. The order ended the prosecution in that court at that stage; it was a trial-court ruling that could be appealed, not an appellate decision on the merits of the charged conduct. The charges concerned Trump’s handling of classified-marked records after leaving office and alleged efforts to obstruct the investigation; those allegations were not adjudicated at trial. Smith’s office announced the Justice Department would appeal. That announcement did not undo Cannon’s order or establish that an appeal had succeeded. Dismissal on those procedural grounds left the allegations untested in a criminal trial.

patch.description_long: On February 27, 2026, Trump told PBS News he was not considering declaring a national emergency around the midterm elections, after reports emerged about a draft executive order circulating among allies. The Washington Post reported that advocates said they were coordinating with the White House, but the existence of such claims does not establish that the White House authored or adopted the proposal. Trump’s denial and the circulated draft are separate facts: at that point, no such order had been issued. A circulated proposal could signal advocates’ goals while remaining distinct from an executive action carrying the president’s approval.

patch.description_long: Sidney Powell, a former Trump campaign lawyer, pleaded guilty on October 19, 2023, in the Georgia prosecution over efforts to reverse the state’s 2020 election result. She admitted six misdemeanor counts of conspiracy to commit intentional interference with the performance of election duties. The plea covered the Coffee County episode: Powell agreed she had paid employees of a forensic firm to travel to the county and copy voter data without authorization, interfering with the election director’s work. The judge sentenced her to six years of probation. Her agreement also required a $6,000 fine, $2,700 in restitution to Georgia, document production and truthful testimony in co-defendants’ trials. Powell’s agreement came one day before jury selection was due to begin, making her the second defendant to plead guilty in the case. Her admitted conduct and cooperation commitments concerned her own plea; they did not decide the charges against other defendants.

patch.description_long: President Donald Trump met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un at Panmunjom on June 30, 2019, during a visit to the Demilitarized Zone between North and South Korea. After greeting one another at the border, Trump briefly crossed the military demarcation line into North Korea, then crossed back into South Korea alongside Kim. The meeting made Trump the first sitting U.S. president to set foot in North Korea. South Korean President Moon Jae-in also joined the encounter on the southern side. The meeting followed Trump’s public invitation to Kim and came after the February 2019 Hanoi summit ended without an agreement. Trump and Kim agreed to restart working-level negotiations over North Korea’s nuclear program. The border crossing was a symbolic diplomatic moment, but it did not itself produce a nuclear agreement or resolve the disputes that had stalled negotiations. The meeting’s public symbolism was distinct from an agreement requiring measurable nuclear disarmament.

patch.description_long: A January 2017 U.S. intelligence community assessment on Russian election activity included a specific, qualified observation about early pro-Trump social media messaging. It said a journalist regarded as an expert on the Internet Research Agency had claimed that some accounts apparently connected to Russian professional trolls—accounts previously used to support Russian actions in Ukraine—began advocating for Trump as early as December 2015. FactCheck.org’s timeline repeats that qualification and identifies the assessment as its source. This early activity should be distinguished from the later, broader operation: the assessment and subsequent indictments describe additional social media content and advertising during the 2016 campaign. Nor does this evidence alone establish coordination with Trump’s campaign. The event can be described as an intelligence-assessment summary of an attributed observation, with its limited scope and attribution preserved. The reporting described an effort to amplify support online while leaving the scale and influence of that activity uncertain.

patch.description_long: On March 31, 2016, Us Weekly published a “new couple alert” alleging that Wendi Deng, Rupert Murdoch’s former wife, and Russian President Vladimir Putin were dating. The Week summarized the item while emphasizing that it rested on rumor; Vanity Fair likewise described it as gossip attributed to Us Weekly and acknowledged that the claim was unverified. The available reports do not name a source with direct knowledge, provide evidence of a relationship, or establish when one might have begun. The TrumpFile timeline adds that Deng was friends with Ivanka Trump, but the dating report itself does not demonstrate any political contact, policy consequence, or involvement by the Trump family. If retained in the catalog, the description should clearly identify the source and uncertainty and avoid implying the rumor proves an association with Trump. Publication gave an unconfirmed claim public visibility without establishing that the two people were in a relationship.

patch.description_long: The Associated Press reported on December 20, 2025, that at least 16 files had disappeared from the Justice Department’s public webpage for records concerning Jeffrey Epstein. The files had been posted less than a day earlier, and one was a photograph showing President Donald Trump. AP reported no government explanation or notice to the public at the time of publication. The report establishes a specific discrepancy between an initial release and the files then visible online. It does not identify the contents of all 16 files, determine when each was removed, or establish who made the decision. Nor does the disappearance by itself show that the records were removed at Trump’s direction or to protect him. That distinction matters: an online file count can document a disclosure problem, while motive and responsibility require additional records or attributable statements. AP’s account described the website at publication, leaving the cause of the missing files unresolved.

patch.description_long:
Trump addressed the Conservative Political Action Conference in National Harbor, Maryland, on March 6, 2014, while considering another presidential run. His speech combined political criticism with accounts of his own businesses. He opened by discussing the Doral resort in Miami, claimed to have spent $250 million rebuilding it and described the project as a source of jobs. The address also criticized U.S. trade relations with China, a recurring theme in his public remarks.

The appearance put Trump before an audience associated with conservative movement politics. He had previously discussed presidential ambitions, so the speech was one episode in a longer record of political positioning rather than a formal campaign launch. Rand Paul won the conference’s 2014 straw poll; speaking at the event did not establish that Trump placed second. The conference appearance documented what he said publicly, while the timing of an organized presidential campaign depended on separate actions beyond the speech.
